# Teaching the Machine {.unnumbered}

\lettrine{I}{n} an offline machine learning benchmark, the dataset is fixed before evaluation. A classifier reads held-out examples drawn from a specified data distribution ($x \sim P_{\text{data}}$); its prediction does not change the next stored example. This useful testing assumption says nothing about a deployed model whose outputs affect people, later data, or physical state.

For a physical machine, the states encountered during execution depend on the actions it actually takes. An accepted motor command changes the plant and can change the next observation ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$, with $a_t$ the executed action). The data distribution is therefore **endogenous** to the closed loop. Training must account for states the learned policy may visit, including recovery states absent from expert-only demonstrations.

::: {#pri-vol4-endogenous-drift .callout-principle title="Endogenous feedback and distribution shift"}

**Invariant**: Executed actions can change later observations ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$), so an expert-only dataset may omit states visited by the learned policy. Let $\pi$ be the learned policy, $\pi^*$ the expert, $J(\cdot)$ expected cumulative task cost over horizon $T$, and $\epsilon$ the probability that $\pi$ disagrees with $\pi^*$ on expert-visited states (0–1 action loss). With per-step task cost bounded in $[0,1]$, behavioral cloning has the worst-case upper bound [@ross2011reduction]:
$$ J(\pi) - J(\pi^*) \le T^2 \epsilon. $$

**Implication**: The quadratic term is a bound that can be tight for some problems, not a trajectory law for every robot. Training can address the state-distribution gap by obtaining expert labels on learner-visited states (as in Dataset Aggregation, DAgger), collecting recovery data through safe perturbations, or learning from validated physical or simulated interaction.

:::

Part II guides students through the three stages of teaching an embodied machine:

* **Data as Physical Experience (@sec-data):** Repeated physical demonstrations wear transmissions, heat motor windings, and use battery energy and operator time. We examine teleoperation and synchronized sensor logging, then distinguish four command taps: requested, mapped, permitted, and measured action. Expert labels or corrective demonstrations on learner-visited states can expose recovery behavior missing from expert-only logs [@ross2011reduction].
* **Policy Training and Coverage Gaps (@sec-training):** We compare behavioral cloning, offline reinforcement learning, and simulation-to-real transfer against the recovery states each training method leaves uncovered. When the same observation admits distinct valid actions, direct mean-squared-error regression can average two safe paths into an unsafe one. Diffusion Policy models alternative action sequences [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]; Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) predicts short sequences of future actions, with temporal ensembling to combine overlapping predictions [@zhao2023learning]. The real-time controller remains responsible for interpolation and actuator permission. We then examine friction hysteresis, compliance, and motor phase lag in transfer to hardware.
* **Evaluation as Closed-Loop Reality (@sec-evaluation):** Offline error on fixed examples does not determine survival after the policy changes which states it visits. Contact, obstacles, and recovery behavior can amplify errors in task-dependent ways. We evaluate the integrated machine through closed-loop trials, exact binomial confidence bounds, and analysis of rare failures and the physical cost of testing.

::: {#pri-vol4-action-chunking .callout-principle title="Multimodal trajectory integrity"}

**Invariant**: Some tasks permit distinct valid actions from the same observation. If demonstrations pass an obstacle on either side, a single mean-squared-error prediction can point into the obstacle between them. This failure depends on the task, observation, and demonstration distribution.

**Implication**: When distinct action modes matter, a conditional generative policy can represent alternatives: Diffusion Policy can sample alternative action sequences [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. ACT predicts action chunks and combines overlapping predictions through temporal ensembling to support temporal consistency [@zhao2023learning]. The downstream controller must still check each proposed action against physical limits.

:::

::: {#pri-vol4-closed-loop-reality .callout-principle title="Closed-loop validation"}

**Invariant**: Error on fixed, expert-visited examples alone does not bound closed-loop survival ($R_{\text{closed}}$). A learned action may move the machine into states absent from that test set; the effect on failures depends on the plant, environment, and independent permission path.

**Implication**: Evaluate the integrated system in closed-loop trials across its stated operating conditions, recording interventions and failures. Exact binomial confidence bounds describe what a finite trial count supports; tail analysis and runtime safeguards address risks that average test accuracy cannot establish.

:::

Part II teaches students to collect physical experience, train action policies for the states they may encounter, and evaluate the resulting closed loop.
